cards.front: Troubleshooting first step when Claude's output disappoints?
cards.back: Name the **symptom**, map it to a likely **cause**, then change the input that addresses that cause. Don't just regenerate.

cards.front: Symptom: generic, could-be-anyone answer. Likely cause and fix?
cards.back: **Missing context.** Add background (who, what situation) or attach the source document or data.

cards.front: Symptom: right topic but wrong length, tone or technical level. Cause and fix?
cards.back: **Vague goal.** State the audience, purpose, length and format.

cards.front: Symptom: good content, but the layout differs every time. Fix?
cards.back: **Show an example** of the exact format (and store it in the Project or template).

cards.front: Symptom: Claude quotes an old policy or price list. Cause and fix?
cards.back: **Stale knowledge.** Replace or remove superseded Project files, keep one current version, and retest.

cards.front: Symptom: Claude forgets rules agreed earlier in a long chat. Fix?
cards.back: **Long thread.** Ask for a summary of decisions and constraints, start a fresh chat with it, or persist the rules in Project instructions.

cards.front: Symptom: output skips parts or muddles steps of a big job. Fix?
cards.back: **Task too big.** Decompose it: get a plan or outline, approve it, then work step by step and check each step.

cards.front: Symptom: shallow analysis on complex work, or slow and costly on trivial work. Cause?
cards.back: **Wrong tool or model.** Switch the feature (chat, Project, Research, Artifact) or the model tier to fit the task.

cards.front: Claude invents a statistic or citation. Best fix?
cards.back: Provide the source, tell Claude to answer only from it and say when something isn't there, then **verify against the original**.

cards.front: Why change only one thing at a time when fixing a prompt?
cards.back: So you know **which change helped** and can reuse it. Changing several things at once hides the cause.

cards.front: Is adding 'be accurate' or 'don't make mistakes' a real fix?
cards.back: No. Claude can't check facts it wasn't given. **Supply the source** and verify.

cards.front: Does asking Claude to rate its own confidence validate the facts?
cards.back: No. Self-rated confidence and confident tone are **not evidence** of accuracy.

cards.front: Will a more capable model fix an output that lacks your company's context?
cards.back: Not reliably. It guesses more fluently, but it still guesses. **Add the context.**

cards.front: What does the Help Center advise about relying on Claude for high-stakes facts?
cards.back: Don't rely on Claude as a single source of truth. Scrutinize high-stakes advice and check cited sources.

cards.front: Two sources of evidence for adjusting your approach (7.2)?
cards.back: 1) The output judged against **clear criteria**. 2) **Feedback from the people who receive it.**

cards.front: You make the same correction to Claude's drafts every week. Best move?
cards.back: Fold it into **durable instructions**: Project instructions, a template, a knowledge file or a Skill. Then retest on past examples.

cards.front: What makes in-chat feedback to Claude effective?
cards.back: Be specific: what to **keep**, what to **change**, and the **target** (audience, length, focus). Not just 'try again'.

cards.front: Simple measures to judge whether a change improved results?
cards.back: Rework rate, checklist pass rate, how much reviewers still edit, and time to a usable draft.

cards.front: After adding a new instruction to a Project, what should you do?
cards.back: **Retest** a few known requests to confirm it fixes the problem and doesn't conflict with existing rules.

cards.front: Signals to stop iterating on the prompt?
cards.back: Several targeted fixes fail the same way; Claude needs data it can't reach; reviewers disagree on 'good'; experts must fix the substance; it must run automatically across tools.

cards.front: Where can you report an unhelpful or wrong response to Anthropic?
cards.back: The **thumbs-down** feedback control in Claude's apps.

cards.front: Efficiency vs effectiveness in workflow optimization?
cards.back: Efficiency = less time, effort and usage. Effectiveness = better outcomes. A real optimization doesn't trade one away for the other.

cards.front: You paste the same style guide and brief into every new chat. Better approach?
cards.back: A **Project** with those files as knowledge and the rules in Project instructions.

cards.front: Usage-friendly prompting habits from the Help Center?
cards.back: Plan the conversation, give clear and complete messages, **batch related requests** in one message, provide all material at once, and refer back instead of repeating.

cards.front: Factors that use your limits faster (Help Center, at the time of writing)?
cards.back: Message length, attachment size, conversation length, tool use (Research, web search), model choice, effort level, Artifacts, and multi-step tasks (code, files, browsing).

cards.front: Why can Project knowledge be efficient for repeated reference?
cards.back: Per the Help Center, Project documents benefit from caching, and **cached content counts less** against limits than new content.

cards.front: Model choice for high-volume, simple, well-defined tasks?
cards.back: The **lightest model that meets the quality bar**. Spot-check, and move up only if quality falls short.

cards.front: Is Research mode the efficient choice for a quick factual question?
cards.back: No. Research is for multi-source cited investigation and uses limits faster. Use regular chat for quick questions.

cards.front: A Skill is useful for…?
cards.back: A repeatable procedure: packaged instructions and resources Claude loads when relevant, so you don't re-explain the steps.

cards.front: Test for 'not a prompt problem'?
cards.back: If Claude gave the perfect answer, could it still not be used (can't be trusted unchecked, can't connect to the system, not allowed)? If yes, escalate or change the approach.

cards.front: Claude needs live data from an unconnected internal system. What do you do?
cards.back: Supply the data manually for now (with review) and escalate for an approved connector or integration. Don't keep rewording.

cards.front: Who handles API integrations, custom connectors or MCP servers?
cards.back: **Developers.** Agentic, multi-tool automation goes to **Architects**.

cards.front: Who handles domain judgment (legal, clinical, HR edge cases)?
cards.back: A **subject-matter expert** as the decision-maker, with Claude assisting.

cards.front: What goes in a good escalation hand-off?
cards.back: The goal, what you tried (prompts, setup, models), 2-3 failure examples, your diagnosis, and constraints (data sensitivity, policy, volume).

cards.front: Typical distractor types in troubleshooting questions?
cards.back: Cosmetic rewording, blind retry or trusting confidence, overreaction (biggest model, rebuild, abandon). The answer is the targeted, proportionate fix.
